analysis.one_liner: Bans trucking companies from running predatory lease-to-own truck programs that leave drivers with no equity.
analysis.headline: The bill has gone nowhere: introduced September 17, 2025, with one cosponsor, sent to the Transportation Committee, then to its Highways and Transit Subcommittee, with no action since.
analysis.plain_summary: Some trucking companies recruit drivers with a lease-to-own deal: the driver leases a truck from the company, pays it off by hauling freight for that same company, and is supposed to own the truck at the end. In practice, drivers can end up controlling nothing — the company sets their pay and routes, and the driver can finish with no equity in the truck or lose what they had built. This bill tells the Transportation Department to write rules within a year banning those predatory programs by interstate motor carriers, and to set up a process letting drivers escape leases that break the rules. The bill has been referred to committee and has gone no further.
analysis.who_benefits: Truck drivers in lease-purchase programs — typically owner-operator hopefuls who lease a truck from the carrier they drive for. The bill would let federal regulators ban arrangements where the carrier controls the driver's work, pay, and debts while the driver accrues no equity or loses the equity they built, and would give drivers a way to be released from leases that violate the rules. Broader effects reach the public indirectly: drivers squeezed by lease payments have an incentive to overwork, which affects highway safety.

how_it_helps.text: It orders the Transportation Secretary to write rules within one year of enactment prohibiting predatory lease-purchase programs by regulated motor carriers.

It defines the problem to cover the whole arrangement, not just the paperwork: carriers that control a driver's work, pay, and debts while the driver gains no equity in the truck — or loses the equity they had built.
It requires a relief process so drivers can be released from the terms of a lease-purchase agreement that a regulator finds violated the new rules.

analysis.who_pays: Motor carriers that run lease-purchase programs would have to change or end those arrangements within a year of the rules taking effect, and could face drivers being released from contract terms found to violate the regulations. Some carriers that use lease-to-own as a recruiting tool would lose that pipeline; carriers running straightforward programs that build real driver equity would be unaffected.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not itself ban anything — it directs the Transportation Secretary to write regulations within a year, so what actually gets prohibited depends on how future regulators define 'predatory' and how strictly they enforce it.
Some lease-purchase arrangements are a legitimate route for drivers to become truck owners, and a broad definition risks sweeping those in along with the exploitative ones.
The relief process only covers agreements entered into after the new regulations take effect, so drivers already trapped in a lease-purchase contract when the law passes would get no escape from it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit for trapped drivers is real: lease-purchase contracts can leave a driver with nothing after years of payments, and debt pressure can push them toward unsafe hours. The costs are modest but genuine — the freight industry argues some lease-purchase deals are a legitimate path to truck ownership, and a broad definition risks outlawing good programs along with bad ones. The bigger design weakness is the relief clause: drivers already locked into a bad contract when the rules take effect would get no way out, so the help reaches only future drivers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which sent it to its Highways and Transit Subcommittee, and nothing has happened since.

narrative.text: Rep. Julia Brownley introduced the bill in the House on September 17, 2025.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
On September 18, 2025, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit, the standard first stop where most bills wait.
One House Democrat has cosponsored the bill, and no committee action, hearing, or floor vote has occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet, because nothing has happened beyond the bill sitting in subcommittee. If it stays there, motor carriers with lease-purchase programs keep operating under current rules.

for.name: Rep. Julia Brownley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its sole sponsor.

for.name: 1 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only cosponsor it has.

sides.party_line_note: Only one Democrat has signed on so far and no Republican has; with no votes or committee action, there is no record yet of how the parties line up.

industries.industry: Motor carriers that run lease-purchase programs
industries.note: Carriers that recruit drivers with lease-to-own truck deals and collect payments from them would face a federal ban on the predatory versions of these programs, plus a relief process for drivers. Some carriers use these contracts to keep drivers hauling at low pay while charging them for the truck.

Carriers with honest lease-purchase or driver-ownership programs could continue under the rules, but the industry would face new federal regulation of driver contracts and recruitment and finance practices, with compliance costs.

analysis.trajectory: Very unlikely to move. It sits in the Highways and Transit Subcommittee with a single cosponsor and no sign of a hearing or markup; most bills at this stage die quietly when the Congress ends.
